nodes.description:
Connect every server `allowed_tools` references, skipping the
test if a required command isn't on PATH, and start the session's
single background event loop.
Close the session.

mcp_config/allowed_tools/cwd describe the MCP server(s) under
test; `model` is any litellm-recognized model string.

Args:
    mcp_config: Path to the `.mcp.json` describing the MCP
        server(s) under test (stdio transport only).
    allowed_tools: `mcp__<server>__<tool>`-style glob patterns
        (e.g. `"mcp__emc2p__*"`). Only servers named by at least
        one pattern are spawned at all; within a spawned server,
        only matching tools are exposed to the model -- there is
        no separate built-in-tool surface to isolate from here,
        unlike a full agentic CLI, since the model only ever sees
        MCP tools in the first place.
    cwd: Working directory each server subprocess is spawned in.
    model: A litellm model string (e.g. `"deepseek/deepseek-chat"`,
        `"claude-sonnet-4-5"`) -- picks both the provider and the
        API key env var litellm looks for.
    extra_env: Extra environment variables every spawned server
        needs beyond a copy of this process's own environment.
    trace_dir: Directory this session's trace file is written
        under. Defaults to `.live_test_traces` under `cwd`, same
        convention as `HeadlessSession`.
    turn_timeout: Seconds to wait for a single `send_turn` call.
    session_timeout: Seconds bounding the whole session's
        wall-clock runtime, across every `send_turn` call combined.
    max_tool_iterations: Passed straight to
        `run_tool_calling_loop`'s own `max_iterations`, per turn.

Open each server's stdio connection and record the subset of its
tools `allowed_tools` actually references, in the OpenAI
tool-call schema `run_tool_calling_loop` expects.

Call one allowed tool and return its result text, or an error
string, for the model to see as its tool-call result.
Close the session and fail the test, with the trace path in the message.
Fail the test, naming whichever of the turn or session deadline actually ran out.
Run one full tool-calling loop for `prompt`, enforcing `timeout` as the authoritative deadline.

Pull queued (coro_factory, future) work items off `self._inbox`
(a thread-safe queue) until a `None` sentinel asks it to stop.
Whether any of `allowed_tools`' patterns actually names a tool on this server.

Queue a coroutine for the background task to run and block for
its result, via a `concurrent.futures.Future`.

Record one model response to the trace file and add its
usage/cost to this session's running totals.

Owns the whole session's async lifetime in one task: connect, every queued turn, then teardown.

See the class docstring for why this can't be split across
separate `run_coroutine_threadsafe` calls instead.

Flush and close the trace file, write out the final usage
summary, and tear down the background connection.

Send one prompt on the ongoing conversation and block for its final reply.

Submits the work to the session's single background asyncio task
(via a thread-safe queue + concurrent.futures.Future) so the real
`mcp.ClientSession` and `run_tool_calling_loop` machinery stay on
the one task that opened them. Every model response and tool
call/result this turn makes is appended to `self.trace_path` as
it happens, the same debugging role `HeadlessSession`'s raw-line
trace plays.

This session's usage so far, summed across every send_turn call.

`cache_creation_input_tokens`/`duration_api_ms` stay 0 for
providers litellm doesn't report them for (most non-Anthropic
ones, including DeepSeek) -- present for shape-compatibility with
`HeadlessSession.usage_summary()`, not populated everywhere.

A time limit that covers a whole sequence of steps, not just one of them, can catch a total that keeps growing even when every individual step, on its own, behaves fine. A limit on just one step at a time could never catch that.

When a file is opened the ordinary way for writing, the program keeps its own separate memory of where in the file to write next -- and that memory can fall behind if the file itself has grown in the meantime. If more than one program, or more than one connection, can write to the same file, one of them can end up overwriting what another has just added, without anyone noticing. Opening the file in "append" mode instead guarantees that every write, from any of them, always lands at the true, current end of the file.

The deadline that actually cuts work off should be enforced right where that work happens, not only estimated by an outer caller -- an outer check can at best guess how long is left; only the code doing the work can stop it exactly on time.

A safety boundary that one background task opens, used for cleanly cancelling work, has to be closed by that exact same task. If a different task tries to use the connection this boundary is protecting, it causes an error. So the connection's entire lifetime -- opening it, using it, and closing it -- all has to happen on that one same task.

Keeping one real connection open and reused for an entire multi-turn interaction, instead of closing and reopening it every turn, is what makes it possible to test a genuine back-and-forth conversation -- not just a string of disconnected one-off exchanges.

When two separate time limits both apply to the same piece of work -- one just for that piece of work, and one for the larger job it's part of -- the real deadline is whichever of the two runs out first.

A series of calls that each start over from scratch isn't really one conversation -- it's a string of separate, one-off exchanges. That's true even if the exact same messages are sent in the exact same order; a real back-and-forth conversation is a single, ongoing, connected interaction.

If a new tool looks and behaves exactly like one people already use, they can switch to the new tool without changing any of their own code. It's built the same way, has the same methods, gives back the same kind of results, and keeps track of its own internal state the same way.

If the same tests had to be called in two different ways depending on which tool is being used, someone would have to write and maintain two versions of the same tests side by side. That's extra work for no real benefit -- the tests would still be checking the same things either way.

emc2p's mission is to be a genuinely useful tool for people building systems where an AI model works with data through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) -- what the project itself calls being "a valuable tool for data-driven MCPs" (see docs/manifest/emc2p.yaml: tool_for_data_driven_mcps). A tool only proves it's actually useful by being tried against the real thing -- a real model, doing real work, through the real protocol -- not by looking right on paper. Every "why" in this file traces back here, one step at a time, and stops: this is the one goal everything else in the file exists to serve.

Leaving something to be wrapped up later, by a separate cleanup step, leaves it unclear which happens first: reporting the failure, or finishing the record it points to. It would be easy to get that order wrong. Finishing the record right at the moment of failure -- and making sure a later cleanup step can safely do nothing if it's already done -- removes that uncertainty.

Refusing an input a piece of code doesn't know how to handle -- rather than silently ignoring it or guessing what was meant -- surfaces a real gap immediately, while it's still cheap to notice and fix, instead of letting it fail confusingly somewhere much later.

A failure message is only as useful as the record it points someone to. Making sure that record is fully saved before reporting the failure means nothing is left half-written by the time someone actually goes to look at it.

A hand-copied version of something lives on its own, separate from the real version it's supposed to match. Nothing forces someone to update the copy every time the real one changes, so over time it quietly falls out of date.

The full record of the conversation so far is kept and managed internally, by whatever is running the model -- not handed in fresh by the caller each time. The caller only ever needs to supply the next new message.
Writing each event to disk right away, instead of holding everything until the end, guarantees that whatever already happened is safely saved by the time something later in that same turn fails.

Running something live against a real model costs money, and running it again won't necessarily give the same result. Being able to point a failure report at a saved record of what actually happened means nobody has to re-run the very thing that just failed.

A live test only helps the project if two things hold: people can actually afford to keep running it, and when they do, they can trust what it tells them -- including a clear, complete picture of what happened when it fails. If either one breaks down, the live test stops doing the one job it exists to do.

Real calls to a live model cost real money and don't always behave the same way twice, so live tests are meant to be run on purpose and only when needed -- not casually or often. Letting the total cost or running time grow without limit, even if no single call ever actually times out, would go against that.

One continuously-running MCP client + agent loop, driven by litellm.

Keeps every spawned server's stdio subprocess and `ClientSession` open
for the whole `with` block, the same way `HeadlessSession` keeps its
single CLI process alive across turns -- so state a server manages (an
opened registry, ...) persists between `send_turn` calls.

Everything MCP/litellm-side is async and runs on a single background
task on its own event-loop thread -- connect, every `send_turn`, and
teardown all execute inside that *same* task, not one task per call
(`mcp`'s stdio transport opens an anyio task group at connect time, and
anyio requires a cancel scope to be exited from the same task it was
entered in -- closing it from a separate `run_coroutine_threadsafe`
task raises "cancel scope in a different task"). A thread-safe queue
feeds work requests into that one task; a `concurrent.futures.Future`
per request bridges each synchronous public method call back to its
result, so callers use this class exactly like `HeadlessSession` --
no `async def test_...` needed.

Parse a `.mcp.json`'s `mcpServers` into one `StdioServerParameters` per server.

Only the `stdio` transport is supported -- the only kind either repo's
own `.mcp.json` uses. `extra_env` is merged onto a filtered copy of
this process's own environment for every server, the same way
`HeadlessSession.extra_env` applies to the single CLI process it spawns.

When something can't run because a thing it depends on isn't installed or available here -- not because the code being tested is wrong -- marking it skipped keeps that distinction visible, instead of reporting a false failure that looks like a real bug.

A model that can only be reached through a general-purpose code library -- it doesn't come with its own ready-made command-line tool that already knows how to talk to it and run it in a loop, the way some other providers offer.

Only exposing the specific tools something actually asked for -- rather than everything a server happens to offer -- keeps what a live test's model can do deliberately scoped, instead of accidentally exercising (or being affected by) capabilities nobody asked to test.

Reporting a failure through the testing tool's own built-in "fail" function makes it show up the same way any other failed test would. It plugs straight into the testing tool's own reporting, instead of making every caller catch and translate an error themselves.

A live test can only be trusted if it uses the real communication method and the real tool descriptions that an actual connected program would see -- not a hand-copied stand-in. If a stand-in didn't quite match the real thing, that mismatch could easily go unnoticed.

Closing and reopening a connection on every call means paying the full setup cost every single time, and it also throws away anything the other end of the connection was remembering about the ongoing interaction -- things a later call might actually need.

A connection, an open file, and a set of running totals only make sense if the same object holding them is reused for every call in a sequence. Anything set up once and needed by every call after that has to live somewhere that outlasts any single call.

Every call's background work is handed off to one single background task that's already running, using a queue to pass the work over and a promise-like object to pass the result back. This means the same open connection can be reused for every call, instead of opening (and paying for) a brand-new connection each time.

The underlying system for managing background tasks ties each safety boundary to the exact sequence of steps that opened it, so that cancelling it always unwinds cleanly and predictably. If a different, unrelated task tried to close a boundary it never opened, that guarantee would break.

An ordinary function call that waits until a turn's reply is ready before returning, instead of an "async" call that runs in the background. It's built to look and work just like an existing tool, `HeadlessSession.send_turn` -- opened and closed the same way, called once per turn, and offering the same kind of usage summary, trace file, and timeouts. Whoever calls it can use it just like any normal function, without needing to write any special async code themselves.

What makes a test worthwhile is the situation and behavior it actually checks. Forcing the test to also deal with unrelated implementation details -- async code, managing background tasks, keeping track of conversation history -- distracts from that, without actually testing anything more.
Testing the real thing directly means there's no separate copy that needs to be kept up to date -- so there's nothing that can drift out of sync in the first place.

A model driving its own tool calls needs to see a failed tool call the same way a real conversation partner would -- as part of the conversation it can react to -- not as a crash that ends the whole exchange before it can even respond.

Keeping a permanent, step-by-step record of exactly what the model and its tools did -- not just the final answer -- makes it possible to figure out what went wrong after the fact, based on what actually happened, including any smaller calls that happened inside that turn.

A single turn can involve several model replies and tool calls happening one after another, over the network, against a real service. Any one of those steps can time out or fail -- and by then, the earlier steps in that same turn have already happened and had real effects.

Building a record's file name from a timestamp and a random component the moment something starts guarantees no two runs -- even ones started in the same second -- ever share a path or overwrite each other's record.
If a model has never actually been tried out using the real tools, in a real live conversation, there's no way to know it will behave correctly once it really is.

A `HeadlessSession`-shaped alternative that is its own MCP client and
its own agent loop, instead of shelling out to an external agentic CLI.

`HeadlessSession` drives a real MCP server through a *provider CLI*
(`claude -p`, `copilot`) that already bundles both an MCP client and an
agent loop internally -- fine for providers that ship such a CLI, but not
every litellm-supported model has one (see docs/manifest/history.yaml:
project_history.mcp_client_session_added for why this exists: DeepSeek's
own CLI, `dsh`, is a week-old one-shot-only developer preview with no
documented streaming output or usage reporting -- not a good fit for
`HeadlessProvider`'s contract). `McpClientSession` owns both halves
itself instead: `mcp.client.stdio`/`mcp.ClientSession` for the real wire
protocol (the actual tool schemas a connected client would see, not a
hand-mirrored copy), and `emc2p.agents.tool_calling_loop.
run_tool_calling_loop` (via litellm) for the model<->tool-call exchange --
so it works with any litellm-supported model, not just DeepSeek.

Same public shape as `HeadlessSession` (context manager, `send_turn`,
`usage_summary`, `trace_path`, `turn_timeout`/`session_timeout`) so it can
be dropped in wherever a downstream project's own fixture currently
constructs a `HeadlessSession`. Requires both the `agents` extra
(`litellm`) and the `mcp` extra (the `mcp` client SDK) -- `pip install
emc2p[agents,mcp]`.

edges.question: Why prioritize real, observable live behavior over passing tests against a fake stand-in?
Why does it matter, for the mission, whether live testing stays affordable to run and its results stay trustworthy?
Why does it matter, for the mission, that a live test can exercise a real, continuous multi-turn conversation?
Why does it matter whether the total cost and time of live tests stays bounded?
Why does it matter whether writing and maintaining live tests stays easy, instead of doubling the work?
Why does it matter whether a test author's attention stays on the scenario, rather than on incidental plumbing?
Why does it matter whether the trace file stays free of silent corruption from concurrent writers?
Why does it matter whether a failure report points to a complete, finished record rather than a possibly-unfinished one?
Why does it matter whether a timeout failure names which budget actually ran out, rather than just saying a timeout happened?
Why does it matter whether an unsupported configuration fails loudly and immediately, rather than being silently ignored or guessed at?
Why does it matter whether a test that can't run here is marked skipped, rather than reported as a failure?
Why does it matter whether a live test's model only ever sees the specific tools it was actually meant to exercise?
Why does it matter whether a deadline is actually enforced by the code doing the work, not just estimated by an outer caller?
Why would testing only a string of disconnected exchanges, instead of one continuous conversation, actually fall short of what the project needs?
Why does the project need to build its code around this fixed background-task rule at all, rather than avoiding needing one shared connection in the first place?
Why does it matter whether a model driving its own tool calls sees a failed call the way a real conversation partner would, rather than as a crash?
Why rely on live exercise instead of building a mechanism that keeps a mock schema in sync automatically?
Why would a hand-copied version of the tool descriptions drift away from the real ones over time?
Why must this live test use the real communication method, instead of a hand-made copy of the tool descriptions?
Why does a model without its own command-line tool still need to be tested live?
Why build a new client from scratch, instead of always using an existing command-line tool to run models?
edges.note: For example, at the time this was written, DeepSeek's own command-line tool (`dsh`) was a brand-new preview release. It could only run one command at a time, and it didn't yet document how to see streaming output or usage numbers.

edges.question: Why does this module exist as its own thing, instead of extending an existing session type to cover more models?
Why is it important to cap the total cost and time of live tests, instead of just trusting each individual limit to keep things in check?
Why avoid spawning a server that nobody's allowed tools actually reference?
Why track running cost and token totals as each response arrives, rather than only computing them when asked for?
Why expose running usage totals mid-session as their own method, rather than only ever computing them once at the end?
Why persist the final usage summary to its own file, rather than it only being available in memory while the session was open?
Why have a time limit for the whole session at all, separate from each individual turn's own limit?
Why does `send_turn` use whichever runs out first, a per-turn time limit or a per-session time limit, instead of only enforcing the per-turn limit?
Why keep the same way of calling it, instead of just updating the existing tests to call it differently?
Why avoid making test code use special async syntax?
Why should the caller not have to keep track of the conversation history themselves, when writing a live test?
Why does this need to look and work exactly like `HeadlessSession.send_turn`?
Why does it keep track of the conversation itself, instead of making the caller pass the whole conversation back in every time?
Why does this support the `with`-block protocol (closing automatically) instead of requiring every caller to remember to close it themselves?
Why does `send_turn` only take one new plain-text message, instead of the whole conversation history?
Why is the trace file opened in "append" mode specifically, rather than the ordinary "write" mode?
edges.note: This was discovered when a call nested inside another had its own output silently overwritten by the outer call's next write to the same file. (See docs/manifest/history.yaml: project_history.trace_file_opened_in_append_mode.)

edges.question: Why save the record one entry at a time, instead of holding it all and saving it once at the end of the turn?
Why does this write the model's response to the trace file the moment it happens, rather than only after the whole turn completes?
Why does everything that happens during a turn matter to the record, if the turn doesn't succeed or fail as a single, all-or-nothing step?
Why does figuring out what went wrong need a full step-by-step record, instead of just the final reply or error message?
Why does `send_turn` write down every model reply and every tool call/result to a file as it happens?
Why would a call nested inside a turn ever need to write into that same file, instead of having its own separate file?
Why does a durable record need a path that's guaranteed not to collide with any other run's?
Why finish saving the record right at the moment of failure, instead of leaving it to a later cleanup step?
Why finish saving the trace and usage record before reporting the failure, instead of reporting the failure first?
Why does this close the session before raising the test failure, rather than raising first?
Why does `send_turn` report failures using the testing tool's own `pytest.fail`, instead of just raising a plain error?
Why does `send_turn` exist at all?
Why does `send_turn` wait for its result instead of running in the background like an async function would?
Why does making this an ordinary, wait-for-the-result call require routing through one shared background task, instead of each call just starting its own background loop?
Why does entering the session start one background thread and event loop for the whole session, instead of creating one per call?
Why does the background task process queued work one item at a time in a loop, instead of each call being handled independently?
Why does submitting work bridge each call through a `concurrent.futures.Future` rather than the caller awaiting the background work directly?
Why must the connection stay on that one already-running background task, instead of a new one for every call?
edges.note: In practice: the underlying connection library opens a group of background tasks the moment it connects.

edges.question: Why does this one task own connect, every queued turn, and teardown, rather than splitting them across separately scheduled work?
Why does closing tear the connection down by queuing a stop signal for that same background task to process, rather than closing the loop directly from the calling thread?
Why must a safety boundary like this be opened and closed by the very same background task?
edges.note: A fixed rule of the underlying background-task library this project relies on, not a choice this project made -- which is exactly why the chain has to ask a different kind of "why" to keep going past this point (see the hub concept that explains this entry).

edges.question: Why is `send_turn` a method that belongs to an object, rather than a plain standalone function?
Why does this exist as a class you construct and hold onto, rather than a set of free functions?
Why must the connection and other session information stay in place across calls, instead of being freshly set up every time?
Why would losing information between calls actually be a problem, rather than just a matter of speed?
Why does this raise an error for any transport other than `stdio`, instead of skipping or guessing at unsupported entries?
Why does this generate the trace file's full name upfront, before the session has actually done anything yet?
Why does this skip the test, rather than failing it, when a required server's command isn't on PATH?
Why does this filter each server's tools down to the ones `allowed_tools` actually references, instead of exposing everything the server has?
Why does this enforce its own timeout, when the caller already computed an outer deadline before calling it?
Why does this return an error message as the tool's result text, instead of raising a Python exception when a tool call fails?
